planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring; needs about 450 chill hours; best used as a pollination and harvest-window companion.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Elah is one of several Israeli-bred low-chill cultivars evaluated by University of Florida researchers as mid-season alternatives to Anna and Dorsett Golden, needing about 450 chill hours to break dormancy reliably. It ripens in mid-summer with smaller, round-to-oblique fruit of medium texture and good eating quality rather than the largest fruit size in the low-chill group. Its value on the Gulf Coast is chiefly as a pollination and harvest-window companion rather than a standalone dessert apple, since it fills the gap between the earliest low-chill ripeners and the later-season Israeli selections.
sources: UF/IFAS Extension — Low-Chill Apple Cultivars for North Florida (EDIS HS764/MG368)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring; needs about 450 chill hours, well matched to Gulf Coast winters.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Maayan was bred by Chanan Oppenheimer at the Rehovot experiment station in Israel specifically for hot, low-chill growing regions, and needs about 450 hours of winter chilling — well matched to Gulf Coast Texas and Louisiana winters. It ripens mid-season, later than Anna, with round-oblong fruit that is yellow with more than half its surface flushed red. The flesh is notably crisp and highly juicy, making it a good fresh-eating choice among the Israeli low-chill introductions. It keeps reasonably well in storage compared to some of its lower-chill counterparts.
sources: UF/IFAS Extension — Low-Chill Apple Cultivars for North Florida (EDIS HS764/MG368)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring; needs only about 375 chill hours, the lowest of the Israeli low-chill group.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Also bred by Chanan Oppenheimer at Rehovot in Israel, Shlomit has the lowest chill requirement of the Israeli low-chill group at roughly 375 hours, blooming as early as March in warm climates. It ripens from late June through mid-July, ahead of Michal, Elah, and Maayan but slightly behind Anna. Fruit is large and round with light-to-medium yellow skin brushed with a rusty red blush over about a quarter of its surface, and the crisp, highly juicy flesh makes it a solid fresh-market choice for Gulf South backyard orchards. It shares bloom timing closely enough with Anna and Dorsett Golden to serve as a useful cross-pollinator.
sources: UF/IFAS Extension — Low-Chill Apple Cultivars for North Florida (EDIS HS764/MG368)

common_name: White Winter Pearmain Apple (Griffin's Pearmain, Historic Low-Chill Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring; needs about 400 chill hours, unusual for such an old heirloom.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. This old American heirloom likely originated as a chance seedling in the central-eastern United States in the late 1700s or early 1800s and was carried west by settlers, becoming known in Texas orchards under the local name Griffin's Pearmain. Its chill requirement of about 400 hours puts it comfortably within reach of most zone 8-9 Gulf Coast winters, unusual for a variety with such deep heirloom roots. The translucent, waxy yellow skin surrounds firm, aromatic flesh often described as honeyed with tropical notes, and the tree is vigorous, precocious, and a reliable pollenizer for other apple varieties planted nearby. It ripens later than the Israeli and Florida-bred selections, giving Gulf South growers a late-season, better-keeping option.
sources: Trees of Antiquity Heirloom Apple Catalog
